sections.heading: Increasing/decreasing behavior from rate of change

questions.q: A function $f$ has average rates of change of $2$ on $[0,1]$, $5$ on $[1,2]$, and $9$ on $[2,3]$. Determine whether $f$ appears to be concave up or concave down on $[0,3]$, and explain.
questions.answer: Since the average rate of change is itself increasing ($2\to5\to9$), $f$ is speeding up as it increases — this is the signature of a concave-up function on $[0,3]$.

questions.q: A different function $g$ has average rates of change of $8$ on $[0,1]$, $5$ on $[1,2]$, and $1$ on $[2,3]$. Classify the concavity of $g$ on $[0,3]$.
questions.answer: The average rate of change is decreasing ($8\to5\to1$), meaning $g$'s growth is slowing down — this indicates $g$ is concave down on $[0,3]$.

questions.q: The graph shows $f(x)=x^3-3x$, which changes concavity at $x=0$.
parts: Describe the concavity of the graph on $(-2,0)$.
Describe the concavity of the graph on $(0,2)$.
State what kind of point $x=0$ represents.
answers: On $(-2,0)$, the curve bends downward (concave down) — the graph lies below its tangent lines there.
On $(0,2)$, the curve bends upward (concave up) — the graph lies above its tangent lines there.
$x=0$ is an inflection point: the location where concavity changes from down to up.

sections.heading: Rate of change of the rate of change

questions.q: Using average rates of change over consecutive equal-width intervals as a proxy for how the function's growth rate itself is changing, explain what it means for a function to be "concave up" purely in terms of consecutive AROC values, without any calculus notation.
questions.answer: A function is concave up on an interval when its average rate of change is itself increasing as you move from left to right across consecutive equal-width sub-intervals — the function isn't just increasing, it's increasing at a faster and faster pace (or decreasing at a slower and slower pace).

questions.q: A company's revenue (in thousands) is modeled by $R(t)=t^3-6t^2+40t$ for $0\leq t\leq10$ years. Find the average rate of change on $[0,2]$ and on $[2,4]$, then determine whether revenue growth is accelerating or decelerating over $[0,4]$.
questions.answer: $R(0)=0$, $R(2)=8-24+80=64$, $R(4)=64-96+160=128$. AROC on $[0,2]$: $\dfrac{64-0}{2}=32$. AROC on $[2,4]$: $\dfrac{128-64}{2}=32$. Since both average rates are equal, revenue growth appears roughly linear (neither clearly accelerating nor decelerating) over this specific interval pair.

questions.q: For the same revenue function, find the AROC on $[4,6]$ and compare it to the AROC on $[2,4]$ found above, to determine the concavity trend as $t$ increases past $4$.
questions.answer: $R(6)=216-216+240=240$. AROC on $[4,6]$: $\dfrac{240-128}{2}=56$. Since $56>32$ (the AROC on $[2,4]$), the rate of change is increasing, indicating the revenue curve is concave up on $[4,6]$ — growth is accelerating in this later interval.

sections.heading: Estimating rate of change from a table

questions.q: A car's odometer reading (miles) is recorded every hour: $t=0$: $120$; $t=1$: $175$; $t=2$: $238$; $t=3$: $310$. Find the AROC over each hour and determine whether the car's speed is increasing, decreasing, or constant.
questions.answer: AROC on $[0,1]$: $175-120=55$ mph. AROC on $[1,2]$: $238-175=63$ mph. AROC on $[2,3]$: $310-238=72$ mph. Since the AROC is increasing each hour ($55\to63\to72$), the car's speed is increasing — consistent with a concave-up distance function.

questions.q: Using the same table, find the AROC over the full interval $[0,3]$ and explain why it differs from the individual hourly rates.
questions.answer: AROC on $[0,3]$: $\dfrac{310-120}{3}=\dfrac{190}{3}\approx63.3$ mph. This is an average over the whole trip, blending the slower early hour with the faster later hour — it necessarily falls between the smallest (55) and largest (72) hourly rates, but doesn't equal any single hourly rate.

sections.heading: Visualizing rate of change on a graph

questions.q: The graph shows $f(x)=\sqrt{x}$, whose average rate of change decreases as $x$ increases.
parts: Find the AROC of $f(x)=\sqrt{x}$ on $[0,1]$ and on $[4,9]$.
Explain how the shrinking steepness in the graph relates to your two AROC values.
State whether $f(x)=\sqrt{x}$ is concave up or concave down, based on this pattern.
answers: The curve rises steeply near $x=0$ and flattens out as $x$ increases, matching the drop from an AROC of $1$ down to $0.2$ — the function is growing, but at an ever-slower pace.
Since the AROC is decreasing as $x$ increases, $f(x)=\sqrt{x}$ is concave down on $(0,\infty)$.

questions.q: A company reports that its costs are increasing, but at a decreasing rate. Sketch what this implies about the concavity of the cost function, and explain your reasoning without using calculus notation.
questions.answer: "Increasing but at a decreasing rate" means the function is going up (each AROC is positive) but each successive AROC is smaller than the one before — this is the definition of concave down. So the cost function's graph rises but bends downward, flattening out over time.
